newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovakia denies U.S. criticised minority policy.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia denies U.S. criticised minority policy.

text.p: Slovak Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik denied on Monday that the United States had criticised Bratislava's treatment of its minorities when he visited Washington last week.

"I can assure you that the question of national minorities was talked about but not in the form of criticism of the approach of the Slovak Republic," said Hamzik, who met Secretary of State Warren Christopher and his deputy Strobe Talbott during his U.S. trip.
"Insofar as the minority policy of Slovakia was mentioned, then I was the only one who spoke on this theme. There was no criticism from the American side during our talks," he told a news conference.

Slovakia has a 600,000-strong Hungarian minority whose treatment has been a constant source of friction with Budapest, even though the two countries have signed a treaty aimed at normalising relations.
The European Union and NATO have made clear that former East Bloc countries must settle disputes with their neighbours before having any chance of joining the Western groupings.
Last Thursday State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said that the United States had been concerned about indications that the Slovak government's commitment to democracy had been weakening.
Asked to elaborate, Burns said: "The concerns have to do with the treatment of several groups in Slovakian society by the Slovak government."
He did not directly name the Hungarian community but referred reporters to the State Department's annual human rights report issued in March which did.

Hamzik said he had reiterated Slovakia's interest in joining NATO during his Washington talks, which also included a meeting with Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs John Kornblum. "NATO is expanding and we want to become members," Hamzik said.

Slovakia's turbulent political scene, including a power struggle between Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar and President Michal Kovac, has raised doubts over whether the country will be in the first group of ex-communist countries joining NATO.
But Hamzik said: "Nobody promised us that we would be in the first wave, but nobody has said so far who would be in it."
Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and possibly Slovenia are tipped as front runners to be in the first wave.
Hamzik took over in August after Meciar replaced former foreign minister Juraj Schenk who had a low profile.
